subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Clara had been married to Anders for five weeks when they moved into the top floor of his parents' house outside Bergen while their own flat was being repaired. Nobody told her the rules, but there were rules. Coffee was at three, not ten past. Boots went on the left rack, never the right. When she loaded the dishwasher, her mother-in-law quietly reloaded it after she left the kitchen. Anders's sister watched Clara slice bread and said, 'Oh, you cut it thick.' Clara began to feel she was sitting an exam she hadn't studied for. One evening, after another reloaded dishwasher, Anders said at dinner, 'Mamma, Clara does it her way, and it works fine. Let's leave it.' His mother paused, then nodded. Clara's shoulders dropped for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where did Clara and Anders move while their flat was being repaired?
qa.a: Into the top floor of his parents' house outside Bergen.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling during her first weeks in the house?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and uneasy, like sitting an exam she hadn't studied for, as her dishwasher loading and bread slicing were quietly corrected.

qa.q: What did Anders do that helped, and how could he keep helping?
qa.a: He calmly backed Clara's way at dinner; he could keep explaining the house habits to her and gently speak up when she is corrected.

qa.q: How might Anders's mother see the dishwasher business?
qa.a: She may see reloading it as simply keeping her kitchen right, not as a judgement, without realising how watched Clara feels.

grounding: A newly married woman joins a household full of unspoken rules, feels evaluated, and is helped when her husband stands beside her.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Three months after the wedding, Hrithik started teaching physics at his in-laws' coaching institute in Indore. The staff room had rules nobody wrote down. Papaji, his father-in-law, always took the first cup of tea. Varun, his wife's elder brother, decided which batches got the air-conditioned rooms. On his first day, Hrithik sat in the chair by the window, and the room went silent. Varun said, 'That's Papaji's chair,' with a smile that wasn't really one. For weeks, Hrithik felt every lesson was being judged through the glass door. Then one evening his wife, Nidhi, came to the staff room and said to her brother, in front of everyone, 'Hrithik's batch scored best in the mock test. Give him a proper room.' Varun shrugged. The next Monday, Hrithik had the corner room.

qa.q: Which subject does Hrithik teach at the institute?
qa.a: Physics.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel during his first weeks at the institute?
qa.a: He felt watched and judged, as if every lesson was assessed through the glass door, after the awkward moment with the chair.

qa.q: What could help Hrithik settle in faster?
qa.a: Asking Nidhi or a friendly colleague to explain the unwritten staff-room habits, and keeping up steady teaching while the family adjusts.

qa.q: How might Varun see Hrithik's arrival?
qa.a: Varun is used to deciding things there, so he may see Hrithik as a newcomer testing the family order, which is why he guards the chair and the rooms.

grounding: A new son-in-law working in his wife's family institute feels watched by settled habits until his wife stands up for him.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Dear Seema,
Two months into married life in Nashik, and I'm still learning the house. Nobody said the lamp in the pooja room must be lit before tea, but Aai's face told me the first morning I got it wrong. My sister-in-law tastes the salt in whatever I cook, just a little, and says nothing. At the Sankranti gathering, three aunts watched me hand out til-gul as if they were marking a paper.
Some nights I cry quietly in the bathroom so nobody hears.
What keeps me going is Nikhil. Last Sunday, when his aunt asked why I still work, he said, 'Because she's good at it, and we decided together.' He also tells me the rules before I trip on them now.
Write soon. I miss our loud chai.
Irawati

qa.q: What must be lit before tea, according to the house's unspoken rule?
qa.a: The lamp in the pooja room.

qa.q: How does Irawati feel at the Sankranti gathering?
qa.a: She feels nervous and self-conscious, as if three aunts were marking a paper while she handed out til-gul.

qa.q: What is Nikhil doing that helps Irawati adjust?
qa.a: He stands up for her in front of the family and now tells her the house rules before she trips on them.

qa.q: What might the sister-in-law be thinking when she tastes the salt?
qa.a: She may be curious or protective of the family's way of cooking, testing the newcomer without realising how judged Irawati feels.

grounding: A new daughter-in-law describes feeling watched in a household of unspoken rules, and how her husband's support helps.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
subtype: Spouse caught between own parents and partner [Actor]
passage: Friday: at dinner, Farhan's mother said Rukhsar should stop working late now that she was married. Rukhsar looked at Farhan. He looked at his plate. His brother Zubin changed the subject to cricket. That night Rukhsar slept facing the wall. Tuesday: his mother complained that Rukhsar never asked her opinion; Rukhsar complained that Farhan never defended her. Farhan felt like a rope pulled at both ends, and he stayed late at the office to avoid them both. The next Sunday: at lunch, Farhan put down his spoon. 'Ammi, Rukhsar's late shifts are our decision, and I'm proud of her work. Rukhsar, Ammi misses you in the evenings. Can we keep Sundays for family lunch?' His mother sniffed, but agreed. Rukhsar squeezed his hand under the table. Zubin grinned at his rice.

qa.q: What did Zubin do when Rukhsar looked at Farhan on Friday?
qa.a: He changed the subject to cricket.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt torn and trapped, like a rope pulled at both ends, so he stayed late at the office to avoid them both.

qa.q: What made Farhan's Sunday stand work?
qa.a: He stated the decision calmly and fairly, backing Rukhsar's work while naming his mother's feelings and offering Sunday lunches.

qa.q: How did Farhan's silence on Friday affect Rukhsar?
qa.a: She felt unsupported and hurt, and slept facing the wall that night.

grounding: Over a week a young husband moves from silent avoidance between his mother and wife to a calm, fair stand that respects both.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
subtype: Spouse caught between own parents and partner [Actor]
passage: Suraj, you think your wife and your parents will sort it out if you keep quiet? Listen to your Binita pishi. When I married your pishemoshai, my father wanted him to join our family tea business in Guwahati. He wanted to stay with his railway job. Every visit, Baba lectured, your pishemoshai went stiff, and I just served more fish. I thought silence kept the peace. It didn't. Baba thought I didn't respect him, and my husband thought I secretly agreed with Baba. Both of them felt alone, and so did I. One Bijoya evening I finally said, 'Baba, he is staying with the railways, and I support him. But we'll come every holiday and help at the garden.' Baba didn't speak to me for a week. After that, things were better than they had been in a year.

qa.q: What job did Binita's husband want to keep?
qa.a: His railway job.

qa.q: Why did young Binita keep serving more fish during the lectures?
qa.a: She was anxious and torn, hoping silence would keep the peace between her father and her husband.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Speaking up on Bijoya evening with a calm, fair stand, backing her husband's job while offering holiday visits and help, so both men knew where she stood.

qa.q: How did Baba feel during those silent years?
qa.a: He felt disrespected and alone, thinking his daughter did not value his wishes.

grounding: An aunt recalls how staying silent between her father and husband left everyone unsupported until she took a calm, fair stand.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
subtype: Spouse caught between own parents and partner [Actor]
passage: The movers wanted to leave by four, the rain was coming in sideways, and Manoj's mother stood in the doorway of the new flat with the key to Dadi's huge carved almirah. 'This goes in the bedroom. It's family.' Kritika, soaked, shook her head. 'There's no space, Mummy. We agreed it goes to storage.' Both of them turned to Manoj. His younger brother Ujjwal, carrying boxes, froze on the stairs. Manoj's first thought was to mumble and let the movers decide. Instead he took a breath. 'Mummy, Kritika's right that it won't fit, and I agreed to storage. But I know it matters to you. Let's store it for now and find it a place when we get a bigger flat.' His mother's lips tightened. Kritika touched his arm. The movers carried the almirah back to the truck.

qa.q: By what time did the movers want to leave?
qa.a: By four.

qa.q: What was Manoj tempted to do when both women turned to him, and why?
qa.a: He felt torn and pressured, and his first impulse was to mumble and let the movers decide, avoiding taking a side.

qa.q: What made Manoj's answer a fair stand?
qa.a: He agreed with Kritika's facts and their earlier decision while naming why the almirah matters to his mother and offering a later plan.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal, frozen on the stairs?
qa.a: He is caught watching a tense family moment, probably uneasy and unsure whether to step in, and relieved when Manoj settles it.

grounding: A young husband caught between his mother and wife on a rushed, rainy moving day chooses a calm, fair stand over silence.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Sahil: Mummy just asked in the family group for our money details again 😅
Charu: Okay. Before we reply, what are we comfortable sharing?
Sahil: That we're doing fine. Not numbers.
Charu: Agreed. And the house-hunting? I'd rather tell them once we've decided.
Sahil: Same. I'll write it, you check?
Charu: Yes. Keep it warm, she means well.
[Family group]
Sahil: Mummy, we love that you care 🙂 We've decided to keep money details between the two of us, but we're managing well, promise. We'll share big news, like a house, as soon as it's final.
Mummy: Hmm. Okay beta. Just worried.
Papa: Sensible.
Bua: Our children are growing up!
[Private chat]
Charu: That went better than I thought 🙏

qa.q: Who wrote the reply in the family group?
qa.a: Sahil wrote it, and Charu checked it.

qa.q: How did Charu feel after the family replied?
qa.a: Charu felt relieved and pleasantly surprised, saying it went better than expected.

qa.q: Which part of how Sahil and Charu handled this worked, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing privately first on what to share, then replying warmly with reassurance; the kind tone made the limit easier to accept.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel reading Sahil's message?
qa.a: She is a little let down and still worried ('Hmm... Just worried'), but the warm tone helps her accept it.

grounding: A young couple agrees together on what to keep private from family and says it kindly, and the family accepts it.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: In Tarun's family house in a small town near Hubballi, doors were never shut. Amma walked into the young couple's room to fold clothes, Atte came in to borrow the mirror, and the nephews ran in at six in the morning. Charu never complained aloud, but she had started changing in the bathroom. One night, Tarun and Charu sat on the terrace and decided together: their room would stay theirs in the evenings and early mornings, and the rest of the house was open to everyone. The next day, Tarun brought Amma a string of jasmine and said, 'Amma, we love that everyone drops in. Can we ask for a knock before eight in the morning and after dinner? It'll help us rest.' Amma laughed, a little hurt. 'In my time, who knocked?' But that evening, there was a soft tap on the door.

qa.q: What did Tarun bring Amma the next day?
qa.a: A string of jasmine.

qa.q: What does Charu changing in the bathroom suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and short of privacy with people walking in, even though she never complained aloud.

qa.q: Which step made the request easier for Amma to accept?
qa.a: Deciding together first and then asking warmly, with jasmine and appreciation for the drop-ins, instead of complaining in anger.

qa.q: How might Amma experience the request?
qa.a: She feels a little hurt, since in her time nobody knocked, but she respects it and taps on the door that evening.

grounding: A young couple agrees together on a privacy limit in a joint household and asks for it warmly, and it is accepted.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Diego's mother, Carmen, had a spare key to their flat in Valencia, and she used it. Twice a week, Tuan came home from his shift to find the fridge restocked, his shirts ironed and the sofa cushions rearranged. He was grateful and also quietly worn out. One Sunday, over coffee, Tuan told Diego how it felt, and Diego admitted he'd been avoiding the subject. They agreed on what they wanted: Carmen keeps the key for emergencies, and she calls before visiting. At the next family lunch, Diego took his mother's hand. 'Mamá, we love your cooking and your help. Please keep the key, but call first, so we can be home and actually sit with you.' Carmen blinked, then laughed. 'So now I need an appointment?' Diego's father said, 'We did the same with my mother.' The next Tuesday, she called.

qa.q: What did Tuan find when coming home twice a week?
qa.a: The fridge restocked, his shirts ironed and the sofa cushions rearranged.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel about Carmen's visits?
qa.a: He was grateful and also quietly worn out, with no say over when she came.

qa.q: What made Diego's request likely to be accepted?
qa.a: The couple agreed privately first, and Diego asked warmly, thanking Carmen and letting her keep the key, only asking her to call first.

qa.q: Why might Diego's father react as he did?
qa.a: He had set a similar limit with his own mother, so he sees the request as normal and helps Carmen accept it.

grounding: A couple agrees together on a boundary about visits and offers it to a parent with warmth, and it is accepted.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: In the hospital waiting room, Tanuja's aunts were arguing about who should sign the forms. Tanuja had just come back from the records desk, where a clerk asked whether 'the other son, Mr Deepak' should be informed too. Her father had no son. Or so she had thought. The aunts' voices rose. Mausi snapped that Tanuja's father had always been careless with family. Tanuja felt the words sitting on her tongue, a way to win the argument in one sentence. She kept quiet. At lunch she found Ishita, the hospital counsellor she knew from college. 'I don't know if it's mine to tell,' Tanuja said. 'Or if Papa should, when he's well.' Ishita asked, 'Who needs to know now, for his care, and who can wait?' That evening Tanuja told only her mother, gently, and they decided to ask Papa together once he was out of danger.

qa.q: Who did the clerk ask about at the records desk?
qa.a: 'The other son, Mr Deepak', whom Tanuja had not known about.

qa.q: What was Tanuja tempted to do during the aunts' argument, and why did she hold back?
qa.a: She felt an angry pull to win the argument by revealing the secret, but held back, unsure it was hers to tell.

qa.q: How did Ishita's question help Tanuja decide?
qa.a: It split the problem into who needs to know now for Papa's care and who can wait, so Tanuja told only her mother.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's mother experience that evening conversation?
qa.a: She hears hard news gently and in private, and is included in deciding how to raise it with Papa, rather than hearing it in a family fight.

grounding: An adult who stumbles on a hard family truth seeks support, weighs who needs to know and does not use it as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Hrithik,
You're the only one I can tell. Last week I found out why my cousin Leena is always so tired. She's sixteen, and she's been washing dishes at a restaurant till midnight, because her father, Uncle Thomas, lost his job in March and hasn't told anyone.
At Sunday lunch, Uncle Thomas was boasting about buying a new car, and my brother joked about 'rich relatives'. I could have said it right there. Part of me wanted to, just to shut him up. I didn't.
That same evening I went to Aunty Sheela, Leena's mother, alone, and told her what I'd seen. She cried, then phoned Leena and brought her home. Now we're quietly helping Uncle Thomas look for work.
I'm not telling the rest of the family. It's his story. But I needed to tell someone. Can we talk tonight?
Jomon

qa.q: How old is Leena?
qa.a: She's sixteen.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel the urge to reveal the secret at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Jomon felt irritated by Uncle Thomas's boasting and was tempted to use the secret to shut him up, but held back.

qa.q: Which step did Jomon take that protected Leena, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Going to Aunty Sheela alone that same evening; it got Leena home quickly without shaming Uncle Thomas in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Uncle Thomas feel if the secret had come out at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: He would likely have felt humiliated and exposed in front of the whole family, making it harder to accept help.

grounding: An adult weighs safety, privacy and fairness in handling a family secret, tells only the person who can act, and seeks a friend's support.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Ramesh, can I tell you something, as a friend? Rafiq's big headache this month. Abbu called me alone last week. He has a heart condition, and he wants to go for surgery without telling my brother or my sisters. 'They'll panic,' he said. So I've been carrying it. Then on Friday my brother shouted at me in front of everyone for not visiting enough, and I nearly said, 'You don't even know Abbu is sick.' I stopped myself. It would have been a weapon, not the truth told properly. I think my sisters have a right to know before the surgery, but it's Abbu's news to give. So tomorrow I'm going to sit with him and ask him to tell them himself, with me right there. Does that sound fair to you?

qa.q: What does Abbu want to do without telling the others?
qa.a: Go for surgery without telling Rafiq's brother or sisters.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when the brother shouted in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rafiq felt angry and hurt, tempted to use the secret as a weapon, but stopped.

qa.q: What is wise about Rafiq's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: It respects that the news is Abbu's to give while being fair to the siblings, by asking Abbu to tell them himself with Rafiq there for support.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's sisters feel if they learned about the surgery only afterwards?
qa.a: They would likely feel shut out and hurt, having had no chance to support Abbu before it.

grounding: An adult holding a parent's hard secret weighs fairness and privacy, confides in a friend and refuses to use it as a weapon.

passage:
'Who can tell me why the ice cube melted faster on the steel plate?' asked Mrs Das.
Jahnavi's hand went halfway up, then stopped.
'Go on, Jahnavi. Half an idea is welcome here.'
'Because... steel is colder?'
Tarun giggled. Mrs Das didn't look at him. 'Interesting. Steel feels colder, doesn't it? Who thinks something else?'
Tarun said, 'Steel passes heat faster?'
'Yes! And Jahnavi's answer helped us get there, because it's what most people think. A great wrong answer.'
Jahnavi grinned. 'So steel only feels cold because it takes heat from my hand?'
'Exactly.'
Later, when Mrs Das asked about wooden spoons, Jahnavi's hand shot straight up.

qa.q: Where did the ice cube melt faster?
qa.a: On the steel plate.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's hand going only halfway up suggest?
qa.a: Jahnavi was unsure and a little nervous about being wrong in front of the class.

qa.q: How did Mrs Das make it safe to be wrong?
qa.a: She welcomed 'half an idea', ignored the giggle, and showed how Jahnavi's wrong answer helped the class reach the right one.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun when Mrs Das doesn't react to his giggle?
qa.a: His giggle gets no attention, so the laughing fades, and he joins in by offering his own idea.

grounding: A child in a warm classroom raises a hand while unsure, because a wrong answer is treated as useful.

passage: In Class 5, I was the kid who never put a hand up. Then Omkar sir came to teach maths. On the first day he wrote a sum on the board, got it wrong on purpose, and waited. Lalit spotted it first. Sir said, 'Thank you! Mistakes are how we find the right way.' After that, whenever someone answered wrong, sir asked, 'What were you thinking?' and usually found something right inside it. Nobody laughed, because sir never did. One day I put my hand up for a fraction question, not sure at all. I said three-fifths. It was three-eighths. Sir said, 'Good, you knew the top part. Now let's fix the bottom.' That's how I, Tanvir, started talking in class.

qa.q: What did Omkar sir do on the first day?
qa.a: He wrote a sum on the board, got it wrong on purpose, and waited.

qa.q: How was Tanvir feeling when raising a hand for the fraction question?
qa.a: Tanvir felt unsure and nervous, not sure at all of the answer, yet safe enough to try.

qa.q: What could other teachers borrow from Omkar sir?
qa.a: Asking 'What were you thinking?' after a wrong answer and pointing out the part that was right, so children keep trying.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when sir thanked Lalit for spotting the mistake?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt proud and encouraged, seeing that catching errors was welcomed.

grounding: A child who never answered starts raising a hand once a teacher treats mistakes as part of learning.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3B, Monday. Rashmi, who joined us from another school in June, had not answered a single question aloud in three weeks. Today, in our reading circle, she raised her hand to guess what 'enormous' meant. She said 'very noisy'. A few children started to smile; Chandrika whispered, 'Remember our rule,' and they stopped. I thanked Rashmi, said noisy things are often enormous, like thunder, and asked the class to help her finish the idea. Chandrika offered 'very big'. Rashmi nodded, smiling. In maths she raised her hand twice more. I will pair Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading, and I'll mention the brave guessing to her mother at pickup today.

qa.q: What guess did Rashmi give for 'enormous'?
qa.a: 'Very noisy'.

qa.q: What does Rashmi raising her hand twice more in maths suggest?
qa.a: She felt safer and more confident after her wrong guess was treated kindly.

qa.q: What did the teacher plan next to build on today?
qa.a: Pairing Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading and mentioning the brave guessing to her mother at pickup.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see her part in the reading circle?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to feel responsible for the class rule, gently stopping the smiles and then helping finish Rashmi's idea.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a quiet new child daring to guess aloud once the class treats a wrong answer kindly.

passage: Note from the Class 6 science teacher, Thursday. Payal used to be the first hand up. Since the quiz on 12 August, when she said the moon makes its own light and Baljeet and a few others laughed loudly, she has not volunteered once. Today I asked her directly about plant roots. She knew it; I saw it in her notebook later. But she said, 'I don't know,' and looked down at her desk. Baljeet glanced at his friends. After class I spoke to Payal alone and told her that her notebook answer was right, and that laughing at answers is not allowed in my room. Tomorrow I will set a class rule about this with everyone, and speak to Baljeet privately first.

qa.q: What did Payal say about the moon at the quiz?
qa.a: That the moon makes its own light.

qa.q: Why did Payal say 'I don't know' when she knew the answer?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at again and felt safer staying quiet than risking embarrassment.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning to do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Set a class rule against laughing at answers and talk to Baljeet privately first, so the class becomes safe again without shaming anyone.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be thinking when he glances at his friends?
qa.a: He may be checking whether they'll laugh again, enjoying the attention, without seeing how much his laughing silenced Payal.

grounding: A teacher's note on a child who stopped volunteering after being laughed at, hiding what she knows to stay safe.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Maths today. Miss asked who could solve the sum on the board. I knew it. I really did. But last week, when I said seven eights are fifty-four, Sonu and his gang laughed so loudly that even the class next door heard. Sonu kept saying 'fifty-four' at lunch all week. So today I kept my hand under the desk. Farida got it right and everyone clapped. I had the same answer in my rough book. I checked after.
Mummy asked why I'm so quiet these days. I said I'm tired. It's easier to be invisible than to be the joke.
Maybe next week.
Irawati

qa.q: What answer did Irawati give last week for seven eights?
qa.a: Fifty-four.

qa.q: Why did Irawati keep a hand under the desk today?
qa.a: Irawati felt scared and embarrassed about being laughed at again, like last week, so staying quiet felt safer.

qa.q: What small step could help Irawati feel safe to answer again?
qa.a: Telling Mummy or Miss about the laughing, so the teacher can stop the mocking in class.

qa.q: How does Mummy likely see Irawati's quietness?
qa.a: Mummy notices it and is concerned, but only hears 'tired', so she doesn't yet know about the laughing.

grounding: A child laughed at for a wrong answer stops volunteering and hides a right answer to avoid being mocked again.

passage: In the government school at Kallur, the English teacher asked Ramesh to read the next line aloud. He read 'Wednesday' as 'Wed-nes-day', the way it looked. The back row burst out laughing, and Harish repeated it in a squeaky voice all through lunch. The next week, when the teacher asked who could read, Ramesh stared hard out of the window at the goats grazing in the field. At home he read his whole English book to his little sister by the lantern, every word, quick and clear. But in class, whenever a question came, he shook his head. The teacher wrote 'shy' in the register and moved on.

qa.q: How did Ramesh read 'Wednesday'?
qa.a: As 'Wed-nes-day', the way it looked.

qa.q: What does Ramesh reading well at home but shaking his head in class suggest?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and afraid of being laughed at again, so he hides his ability in class.

qa.q: What could the teacher do instead of writing 'shy' in the register?
qa.a: Stop the mocking, speak to Ramesh privately, and give him a safe chance to read, perhaps to the teacher alone first.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's little sister see him?
qa.a: She hears him read quick and clear every night, so she likely sees him as a good reader, unlike his classmates.

grounding: A village boy mocked for a mispronunciation stops speaking in class, and his real reading ability goes unseen.

passage: The drilling next door started at nine, and Mrs Mathew had to raise her voice over it. Joseph sat by the window and watched her the way he always did. When Aadhya read her essay aloud and mixed up 'there' and 'their', Kevin snorted. Mrs Mathew stopped the whole class, drill and all. 'Kevin, in this room we don't laugh at mistakes. You'll get the same kindness when you try.' Then, to Aadhya, 'Your idea about the stray dog was the best part. Carry on.' Joseph noticed she used the same calm voice for Kevin as for everyone. Later, when the drill made Priti lose her place and someone began to giggle, Joseph heard himself say, 'We don't laugh at that.'

qa.q: What did Aadhya mix up in her essay?
qa.a: 'There' and 'their'.

qa.q: What was Joseph noticing and feeling as he watched Mrs Mathew?
qa.a: Joseph was paying close attention and seemed reassured and impressed that she used the same calm voice for Kevin as for everyone.

qa.q: What in Mrs Mathew's response is worth copying?
qa.a: She stopped the mocking at once, stayed calm and fair, and praised the strongest part of Aadhya's work.

qa.q: What might Mrs Mathew be hoping for when she stops the class, even with the drill going?
qa.a: She likely wants every child to feel safe making mistakes, knowing that if one snort passes, others will copy it.

grounding: A child watches a teacher stop mockery quickly and fairly on a noisy day, and then copies her in class.

passage: In Class 4C at a Pune municipal school, Irfan watched Usha ma'am's face more than the blackboard. He could tell a lot from it. When Karan, the class monitor, talked during the test, she took his paper away for a minute, exactly as she had done with Irfan's bench-mate Sunny the day before. Same rule. When Sunny finished a sum after three wrong tries, she tapped his notebook and said, 'Three tries! That's how brains grow.' Irfan saw Sunny sit up straighter. And when two girls rolled their eyes at a new student's accent, ma'am only said, 'Eyes to the board,' very quietly, and it stopped. By Friday, Irfan noticed the whole class saying 'Three tries!' to each other whenever someone got stuck.

qa.q: What did Usha ma'am do when Karan talked during the test?
